To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

azole resistance in clinical Candida albicans isolates is a complex process that involves several genetic mechanisms, including point mutations, loss and redupication of the entire chromosome, and isochromosome 6L.
the development of azole-resistant C. albicans strains is associated with the acquisition of hyperactive alleles of the transcriptional regulator TAC1 and of mutations in the target of azoles, ERG11.

azole resistance in the human pathogenic fungus C. albicans was due not only (i) to the presence of mutations in azole-resistance genes (at least TAC1 and CDR1) but also (ii) to their increase in dosage by loss of heterozyosity at the TACI locus and to the addition by isochromosome formation of extra copies of Chr 5.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the genotypes that lead to azole resistance in clinical C. albicans isolates.
the genotypic evolution of azole resistance mechanisms in Candida albican.
the genotypic evolution of azole resistance mechanisms in sequential isolates.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

azole resistance in this species is not only a matter of point mutation but also a complex process involving the acquisition of several mutations, the increase in copy number of genes, and the addition of extra copies of the entire chromosome.
the acquisition of TAC1 GOF alleles is the most important step in azole resistance development.
TAC1 is the main target for azole resistance in the majority of azole-resistant strains.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the evolution of C. albicans to azole resistance is a multistep process that involves the acquisition of multiple genetic modifications, each of which may contribute to azole resistance.
the evolution of azole resistance is a complex process that can be achieved by multiple mechanisms, and the presence of a single mechanism is not sufficient to explain resistance in all strains.

azole resistance can be acquired by a combination of mutations in genes encoding azole targets and by chromosomal rearrangements leading to the amplification of the corresponding chromosomal regions, including TAC1.
The main takeaway from our work is that

C. albicans, a diploid organism, has developed mechanisms to increase the copy number of genes involved in drug resistance, which are not only located on the same chromosome but also linked to each other.
C. albicans can acquire multiple azole resistance mechanisms, including hyperactive TAC1 alleles, ERG11 mutations, and i(5L), which can be combined to achieve high azole resistance levels.

the development of azole-resistance in Candida albican is not a simple process, but is rather the consequence of a complex interplay of several mechanisms, including point mutations in target and efflux genes and chromosomal alterations.
